youtube.aciklama:
Why does a system vibrate more strongly at certain frequencies, and how do filters shape sound? In this lesson we learn resonance and the roles of mass, stiffness and damping, low-pass, high-pass and band-pass filters, cut-off frequency and slope, the limits of octave and one-third octave bands, and how they are used in the clinic.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Speaks, Introduction to Sound: Acoustics for the Hearing and Speech Sciences; Rosen and Howell, Signals and Systems for Speech and Hearing; Gelfand, Hearing: An Introduction to Psychological and Physiological Acoustics; Dillon, Hearing Aids; IEC 61260, Electroacoustics: Octave-band and fractional-octave-band filters.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn why a system vibrates more strongly at certain frequencies, that is, resonance.
Then we will look at types of filters, the cut-off frequency, and the octave bands used in noise measurement.
Every object has one or more natural frequencies at which it vibrates most easily when struck.
When a system is driven at its natural frequency, the vibration amplitude grows clearly; this is called resonance.
Pushing a swing higher by pushing at just the right moments is the best-known everyday example of resonance.
In the graph, you see the vibration amplitude peak at the resonant frequency of one thousand hertz.
If the friction in the system, called damping, is light, the peak is narrow and sharp; as damping increases, the peak gets lower and wider.
A system with a sharp resonance is very selective, but it keeps ringing for a while after the input stops.

ogeler.metin: Square root of stiffness over mass

cumleler: We can think about what sets the resonant frequency with a simple spring and a mass on its end.
The stiffer the spring, the faster the system vibrates; more stiffness raises the resonant frequency.
The larger the mass, the slower the system vibrates; more mass lowers the resonant frequency.
The resonant frequency is proportional to the square root of the ratio of stiffness to mass.
The same principle applies in the middle ear; we will see how stiffness and mass shift middle ear resonance in the immittance lessons.
Air-filled tubes and cavities also resonate; the size of the cavity sets the resonant frequency.
In a tube closed at one end and open at the other, the lowest resonance is where a quarter wavelength equals the tube length.
The ear canal is such a tube, so it provides a natural boost around two thousand five hundred to three thousand hertz.
In a tube open at both ends, the lowest resonance is where half a wavelength equals the tube length.
In speech, the vocal tract from the larynx to the lips also acts like a tube closed at one end, and it creates the formants.
Hearing aid tubing and earmold canals also create their own resonances; these peaks show up in the device's frequency response.
A filter is a system that passes some frequencies and weakens others; it can be an electronic circuit, software or a cavity.
A low-pass filter passes sounds below its cut-off frequency and weakens those above it.
A high-pass filter does the opposite; it passes frequencies above the cut-off and weakens those below.
The cut-off frequency is the point where the output drops three decibels below the passband; here the power is halved.
How quickly a filter weakens sound beyond the cut-off is called its slope, given in decibels per octave.
The simplest, first-order filter has a slope of six decibels per octave; the higher the filter order, the steeper the slope.
The two filters in the graph cross at one thousand hertz and weaken sound by twelve decibels per octave away from the cut-off.
A band-pass filter passes only the band between two cut-off frequencies.
The frequency in the middle of the band is the center frequency, and the difference between the two cut-offs is the bandwidth.
The ratio of center frequency to bandwidth is called the quality factor, or Q; the higher the Q, the more selective the filter.
A band-stop filter weakens a narrow band and passes the rest; a very narrow one is called a notch filter.
The audiometer's narrowband noise is made by passing white noise through a band-pass filter around the test frequency.
Every resonating system is in fact a band-pass filter; a sharp resonance means a narrowband filter.
The curve that shows how much a system boosts or weakens sounds at different frequencies is called its frequency response.
To measure it, the system is given sound at the same level at each frequency, and the output level is recorded.
A flat frequency response passes all frequencies equally; this is what we expect from a good measurement microphone.
Real systems show resonance peaks and filter slopes; this example is illustrative.
The middle ear also acts like a band-pass filter; it transmits mid frequencies most efficiently and very low and very high ones less so.
You will often see these curves in the technical sheets of earphones, microphones and hearing aids.
An octave is the interval over which frequency doubles; for example, five hundred to one thousand hertz is one octave.
In sound measurement, the frequency range is usually divided into octave bands.
The upper limit of each band is twice its lower limit, and the center of the band is the geometric mean of the two limits.
The octave band centered at one thousand hertz covers about seven hundred seven to one thousand four hundred fourteen hertz.
To find the limits, the center frequency is divided and multiplied by the square root of two, about one point four one four.
For finer analysis, one-third octave bands are used; each is one third of an octave wide.
The one-third octave band centered at one thousand hertz spans about eight hundred ninety one to one thousand one hundred twenty two hertz.
The audiogram frequencies of two hundred fifty, five hundred, one thousand, two thousand and four thousand hertz are also one octave apart.
The center frequencies of octave and one-third octave bands are defined in international standards.
The table shows the limits of the octave bands centered at two hundred fifty and one thousand hertz.
In hertz, bandwidth grows with frequency; the four thousand hertz octave band is more than two thousand eight hundred hertz wide.
But the ratio is constant: an octave band is about seventy one percent of its center, a one-third octave band about twenty three percent.
This constant-ratio structure also suits our ear, which perceives frequencies as ratios.
The ear itself works like a filter bank; each region of the cochlea is a narrow band-pass filter.
The width of these auditory filters is the critical band, which we will cover in detail in the lesson on masking and the critical band.
Above the low frequencies, one-third octave bands roughly match classic critical bands; the equivalent rectangular bandwidth is narrower.
In a normal ear, auditory filters are narrow and sharp; with cochlear damage they widen, which means frequency selectivity drops.
This widening is one of the reasons why understanding speech in noise is harder for people with cochlear hearing loss.
We meet these concepts in the clinic every day.
The audiometer's narrowband noise is produced with a band-pass filter centered on the test frequency.
In noise measurement, the octave or one-third octave filters of a sound level meter show where the energy is concentrated.
The maximum permitted background noise in a test booth is also given in standards by octave or one-third octave band.
Hearing aids also split incoming sound into channels with a filter bank and apply separate gain in each channel.
When the ear canal is blocked by an earmold or device, its natural resonance is lost; this loss is accounted for in fitting.

sahneler.metin: The tubing of a behind-the-ear aid is also a resonating tube. If you see sharp peaks in real-ear measurement, check the tubing, earmold canal and acoustic damper.
cumleler: A tip from practice: the tubing and earmold canal of behind-the-ear aids also form a resonating tube.
These resonances can create clear peaks in the device's frequency response, often near one thousand, three thousand and five thousand hertz.
An acoustic damper placed in the tubing smooths these peaks and helps the sound feel more natural.
If you see sharp peaks in real-ear measurement, first check the tubing, the earmold canal and the damper.

maddeler.metin: Octave band: upper limit _twice the lower_

cumleler: The resonant frequency rises with stiffness and falls with mass; damping sets the width of the peak.
Filters are described by their cut-off frequency and slope; the cut-off is where the output drops by three decibels.
In an octave band, the upper limit is twice the lower limit; a one-third octave band allows finer analysis.
The cochlea and hearing aids split sound into frequency bands, like a filter bank.

sahneler.soru: The octave band centered at 2000 Hz?
sahneler.aciklama: The center frequency is divided and multiplied by _the square root of two_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what are the approximate limits of the octave band centered at two thousand hertz?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: one thousand four hundred fourteen to two thousand eight hundred twenty eight hertz.
The center is divided and multiplied by the square root of two; option C is the one-third octave band with the same center.
